failures.title: SEAT CHHB Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Carbon Buildup on Intake Valves - 2013-2018 models
items.whatHappens: The CHHB uses direct injection (TSI), which means fuel is injected directly into the combustion chamber rather than onto the intake valves. This prevents the natural cleaning effect that port injection provides, leading to carbon deposits building up on the intake valves over time. Symptoms include rough idle, loss of power, misfires, and increased fuel consumption.
items.repairVsReplace: This is resolved through walnut blasting or chemical cleaning of the intake valves, a standard maintenance procedure for direct injection engines. It rarely requires a full CHHB replacement unless severe carbon buildup has caused valve damage or piston contamination.

items.title: High-Pressure Fuel Pump (HPFP) Wear
items.whatHappens: The high-pressure fuel pump that delivers fuel at up to 200 bar for the direct injection system can wear over time, particularly if lower-quality fuel is used or service intervals are extended. Symptoms include hard starting, loss of power under load, and fuel pressure error codes.
items.repairVsReplace: The HPFP can be replaced independently without removing the engine. If left unaddressed, a failed HPFP can cause lean running conditions that may damage the catalytic converter or cause misfires, but it rarely writes off the CHHB engine itself.

items.title: Turbocharger Wastegate Rattle
items.whatHappens: The turbocharger wastegate actuator can develop play over time, causing a metallic rattling noise on deceleration or at idle. This is a common issue on many VW Group 2.0 TSI engines.
items.repairVsReplace: Early-stage rattle can sometimes be addressed with actuator adjustment or replacement. If the turbo shaft or bearings are damaged, a full turbo replacement is required, but this is a component-level repair that does not necessitate a full CHHB replacement.

failures.goodYearsLine: The CHHB benefits from the EA888 Gen3 architecture, which resolved the timing chain tensioner issues that plagued earlier EA888 Gen1 and Gen2 engines. The timing chain on the CHHB is far more robust, and catastrophic chain failure is rare when proper oil change intervals are maintained .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the CHHB
variants.intro: The CHHB engine code is physically stamped on a metal tag located on the engine block near the bell housing, but it is most reliably verified via a VIN decoder or by checking the build sheet on your V5C registration document. Owners frequently confuse the CHHB with other 2.0 TSI variants in the VW Group family. Fitting the wrong revision will result in ECU mapping mismatches, incorrect turbo actuator calibration, and persistent limp mode. Common confusable codes include: - CJXG - The 300hp variant fitted to the Leon Cupra 300; uses a larger turbocharger and different ECU calibration. - CHHA - The 265hp variant fitted to the Leon Cupra 265; shares the same block but uses a smaller turbocharger and different mapping. - CJXB - The 210hp variant fitted to the standard Leon FR; significantly lower output and different turbo plumbing. - EA888 Gen3 variants - The broader VW/Audi family that shares the same core architecture but with different calibrations and hardware.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement CHHB Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used CHHB engine only makes financial sense if it comes with documented proof that the carbon cleaning has been performed recently and that there is no audible turbo wastegate rattle. Performance engines like the Cupra variants are often driven hard, so service history is critical.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper CHHB recondition addresses the core wear points of this engine: the block is stripped, the turbocharger is inspected or replaced, the high-pressure fuel pump is checked, and the intake valves are professionally cleaned. This is the most sensible route for a Leon Cupra where performance and reliability are paramount.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full CHHB rebuild is typically only justified for high-mileage Cupra examples or if the engine has suffered catastrophic failure such as timing chain jump or severe carbon-induced valve damage. A rebuild will include upgraded components and comprehensive testing to permanently eliminate any factory weaknesses.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Our network handles the entire CHHB supply and fit process, including ECU coding and immobilizer alignment, backed by a nationwide 12-month warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The CHHB sits in SEAT Leon Cupra chassis, which typically retain values between £8,000 and £18,000 depending on age, mileage, and specification (Cupra 280 vs Cupra 290). Because a reconditioned CHHB supply cost starts around £2,800, the replacement cost represents approximately 20-35% of the vehicle's value, making it a financially viable investment for most examples. However, if your Cupra is showing significant suspension wear, interior deterioration, or has exceeded 120,000 miles, evaluate the overall condition before committing to a replacement.

items.answer: A reconditioned SEAT CHHB engine costs between £2,800 and £4,500 for supply only, or £3,450 to £5,410 fully fitted by an independent specialist. Used units start around £1,500 but carry inherent carbon buildup and turbo risks. Full rebuilds range from £4,200 to £6,500 supply only. Labour typically adds 10-14 hours at £65-£90/hr.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the CHHB engine?
items.answer: The dominant failures are carbon buildup on the intake valves and high-pressure fuel pump (HPFP) wear, typically occurring between 40,000 and 100,000 miles. Direct injection prevents fuel from washing the intake valves, leading to severe carbon deposits that cause rough idle and misfires. The HPFP can also wear prematurely, causing fuel pressure errors and loss of power under load. Both issues are well-understood and can be resolved without replacing the entire engine if caught early.

items.question: Which SEAT models use the CHHB engine?
items.answer: The CHHB was fitted exclusively to the SEAT Leon Cupra 280 and Cupra 290 (5F chassis) between 2013 and 2018. It produces 280 hp (206 kW) or 290 hp (213 kW) and 350 Nm of torque. It is the definitive performance engine for the Mk3 Leon lineup. Always verify fitment, as the Leon FR and standard models use lower-output variants like the CJXB.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned CHHB engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned CHHB is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the inherent carbon buildup and HPFP wear risks of direct injection engines. Used engines rarely come with documented proof that the intake valves have been walnut blasted and the HPFP tested. Reconditioned units are stripped, the carbon is professionally cleaned, and the HPFP and turbo are thoroughly inspected or replaced as standard.

items.answer: The exact engine code is stamped on a metal tag on the engine block near the bell housing and is definitively listed on your V5C registration document or via a VIN decoder. The CHHB is the 280-290hp variant fitted to the Cupra 280/290. The CHHA is a lower-output variant (265hp) and the CJXG is the 300hp Cupra 300 variant. Fitting the wrong revision will result in ECU mapping mismatches, incorrect turbo actuator calibration, and persistent limp mode.
